intro: Clients ask why do architects charge so much because they often view design as a commodity rather than a service. This perception gap leads to fee compression, unpaid overtime, and significant practice burnout.
tldr: Clients focus on price when they do not understand the value of your design process.
Fee compression is a structural issue linked to a lack of business training in architecture education.
You can justify your fees by breaking proposals into distinct, value-based project stages.
Tracking your actual time spent on tasks is essential for accurate, data-backed fee proposals.

blocks.text: The root of the fee justification problem

The question of why do architects charge so much is rarely about the money itself. It is usually about the lack of perceived difference between one architect and another. When you present a proposal that focuses only on deliverables like drawings and meetings, the client treats it like a commodity. They compare your price to the next architect and choose the lowest one. You must shift the conversation from what you provide to what you solve.
Why clients struggle with your fees

Clients often do not see the hours you spend behind the scenes. They see the final render or the building permit, but they miss the technical coordination, the code reviews, and the endless email chains with contractors. If they cannot see the effort, they assume it is easy. Your job is to make the invisible work visible.

items: Use stage-based fees to show the client exactly what they are paying for at each project phase.
Calculate your true overhead costs so you know your minimum viable rate before you start a negotiation.
Ask questions about the client's goals rather than just their requirements to position your work as a solution to their business problems.
Track your time religiously to identify where scope creep is eating your profit margins.

blocks.text: If you use a Mac, you have access to tools that make tracking easier. Apps like Timing allow for automatic background tracking. You do not have to remember to start or stop a timer. It logs what app you use and what file you have open. This data is your best defense when a client asks for a fee reduction. You can show them exactly where the time went.

faq.question: Why is it so hard to negotiate architecture fees?
faq.answer: Most architects are trained in design but not in business or sales. When clients push back on price, many architects feel defensive rather than curious about the client's underlying budget constraints.

faq.question: How can I stop scope creep?
faq.answer: Scope creep happens when the project boundaries are not clearly defined. Break your work into specific, deliverable-based stages. If a client asks for something outside that stage, you can point to the contract and discuss an additional fee for the new work.

faq.question: Does Lazur help me track my time?
faq.answer: Lazur helps you stay focused by answering questions about your software and dictating notes. It does not track your time automatically, but it can help you draft emails to clients explaining the status of a project.

causes.title: Commoditization
causes.text: Clients view design as a standard product rather than a unique service.

causes.title: Lack of business training
causes.text: Architects are rarely taught how to calculate overhead or negotiate complex contracts in school.

fixes.title: Value-based proposals
fixes.text: Stop selling drawings and start selling the benefits of your design solutions.

fixes.title: Time tracking
